As my colleague says, the Government is doing what the Liberals did. Furthermore, the Conservatives are reducing the percentage of the federal Government share in health care.
Rather than cutting its investment in health care, the Government should be investing in long-term health care by finding new ways of delivering health care and improving medicare in this country so that we can reduce the costs in the long term. However, we cannot take the long-term view without being willing to invest in the short term. By cutting now we rob ourselves of the opportunity to re-tool the medicare system and improve it so that it can be more cost-effective than it is today.
I call upon the Government to reconsider its program of cuts to planned expenditures for health care and for post-secondary education.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take part in the debate on Bill C-96 this afternoon and join all those who have spoken to oppose the way this Government is treating the Canadian provinces.
Bill C-96 concerns the joint financing of established programs by the federal Government and the provinces to pay the costs of post-secondary education, hospitalization and

May 5, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
medicare. We all know that the Canadian Government uses a system of redistribution to give money back to the have-not provinces, thanks to the taxes collected from all Canadian provinces. Through this equalization system, the Canadian Government uses the collective wealth of the country and redistributes it equitably amongst the have-not provinces.
However, Bill C-96 under consideration will radically reduce the amounts paid by the Canadian Government to the provinces during the next six years. I have here a table which shows that, during the next six years, between 1986 and 1992, the federal Government will reduce its contribution for post-secondary education, hospitalization and medicare by about $8 billion, or $8,133 million to be exact.
Of course, such a consequence bears heavily on all Canadian provinces, but especially so on the Province of Quebec. Indeed, this will entail a dead loss of about $2 billion over the coming years for the taxpayers and the people of Quebec. Two billion dollars is an abstract figure that people cannot readily appreciate. Just to illustrate: this is equal to two thousand million dollars. Or again, for those who dream of winning $1 million at the lottery, it is in fact nearly $6 million a day that will be lost by for the Province of Quebec over the next six years.
Therefore, it is clear that those $2 billion mean a huge loss for the Quebec Government's coffers. And I cannot but wonder how we can now have this Tory Government reduce the payments that would normally be transferred to the Province of Quebec, without there being one single Conservative Member from Quebec to rise and defend the interests of Quebecers, to prevent such a measure from being passed by this Government.
Where are the Ministers from Quebec on this issue? In particular, where is the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), who boasts about being a great nationalist, a great champion of the interests of Quebec? Where is he? What will he be doing to stop that kind of discriminatory move against Quebec? Where is the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) who was so assertive when he sat in Opposition, but has become so silent since he is sitting on the Government side?
Where are those Ministers, the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Bouchard) and the Minister of State for International Relations, those two who supported the "Yes" option and promised to unswervingly defend Quebec's interests at the federal level? It seems to me they are so speechless, if not totally absent from this debate in which the interests of all Quebecers are at stake.
What I find especially disgusting about that measure, which of course will be approved because of the Government's overwhelming majority-since despite every effort by Opposition Members, the measure will inescapably pass when the Tory steamroller of that silent majority comes around to approve the Bill. But what I want to say before we are run over by the steam roller is that it is a unilateral measure against the interests of the provinces, because the Ottawa Government has never negotiated this cut, never having brought the provinces to the negotiating table to reach a decision which would be acceptable
both to the provinces and the central Government. No, Mr. Speaker.
This is a unilateral decision of the Conservatives who have decided to reduce the amounts that are provided every year to the provinces. Yet, Hon. Members will remember that at the time the Conservatives were sitting on Opposition benches, they had promised never to treat the provinces in this way. They would insist that the word "unilateral" would be banished from the Conservative vocabulary. It is therefore very sad, when one considers what they are doing with Bill C-96, to realize that this is a unilateral measure which will severely affect the Quebec economy.
What is even more serious-and I want to emphasize this as I am about to run out of time-is that this Conservative Government is introducing this legislation at a time when we learn that it has betrayed the commitment it had made last year to the province of Quebec concerning Bill C-39 which it had introduced in the House to provide supplementary fiscal equalization payments, and I quote the comments made at the time by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) on behalf of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), as reported in Hansard on April 18, 1985, and I quote:
The equalization program now protects provinces against declines in payments from one year to the next in a way which varies with their capacity to raise revenues. The highest protection, the 95 per cent floor, is given to those provinces which are not as strong fiscally as others and ensures their payments will decline by no more than 5 per cent from one year to the next.
Well, we have just learned from the Quebec Minister of Finance, on the occasion of his Budget speech, that in fact the Conservative Canadian Government has not kept its promises. And it is not 95 per cent it has granted the Province of Quebec, but 92.8 per cent, which will mean a loss of $66 million for the year ending March 1986. Yet, the Minister of Finance himself, in reply to a question from one of my colleagues on this side of the House, had made the following statement on April 1, 1985, and I quote:
I would like to respond to that question by saying that what we were trying to do was to provide a fair resolution to a difficult problem and one which was considerably more difficult for the Provinces of Quebec, Manitoba and Nova Scotia because they were going to suffer an absolute shortfall. In taking into account this principle of fairness, we decided that we should establish some rationale for dealing with the shortfall. That was, as I indicated in my remarks, to establish a 95 per cent floor for the three provinces-
-which will benefit.
Mr. Speaker, as I said before, the Conservative Government broke the promise it made in April 1985. Over the past fiscal year alone, the Conservative Government has made Quebec lose $66 million which the Quebec Minister of Finance will have to find elsewhere. And on top of everything, to put the icing on the cake, today we are faced with a Bill that will cause the Province of Quebec to incur a loss of $2 billion within the next six years.
This is shameful and scandalous, and I think the silence of our Conservative Members from Quebec on this issue is
May 5, 1986

absolutely unconscionable. Where are they? Why are they silent? And how come there is not a single Minister from the Province of Quebec here in the House, at this very moment, to rise and defend the interests of the Province of Quebec and its people?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-96 today. The title of this Bill is a rather lengthy one and it is one that, quite frankly, very few people understand or have knowledge of. The Bill is entitled an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977.
The Act to which the title of the Bill refers assists provinces in providing hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care and grants for post-secondary education. The Bill itself consists of some five pages. The effect of this Bill will be that each one of those pages will cost something like $1 billion in terms of the provinces' ability to finance the programs I have just mentioned. The effect of this Bill will be to chop in excess of $5 billion over the next four or five years from those programs.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) argued in support of his actions by saying that these measures are designed to moderate the growth rate of payments to the provinces. I suppose that is the newspeak of the late 1980s. In fact, these measures will reduce the ability of many provincial Governments to provide good quality medical care and post-secondary education. Canadians who live in Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland will be entitled to receive a lower quality of health care than those living in British Columbia or one of the better-off provinces. That is what this Bill means. It is a direct attack on medicare and post-secondary education.
I remember that not too many years ago, the then Liberal Government tried to do exactly the same thing. What the Conservative Government is doing today is a continuation of what the Liberal Government tried to do before it was defeated. I am quite sure you will be interested to know, Mr. Speaker, that when the Liberal Government introduced that legislation, the very Hon. Members who are now on the opposite side and are proposing to do exactly the same thing were highly critical of what the then Government was doing. On February 1, 1982, the now Minister of Finance said the following in the House of Commons:
The Minister is prepared to cut spending in two very important areas. He is prepared to risk major cut-backs in medical care and post-secondary education.
Rather than rush into this on a unilateral basis and force spending cuts and service cuts on the provinces, would the Minister consider entering into two or three national conferences on health and post-secondary education so that we can set out the national objectives of the various levels of Government in these two important areas before we cut spending, and before we cause closures of hospitals and cut-backs in post-secondary education?
The question that begs to be answered is, why did the Minister of Finance not do exactly what he felt the Liberal
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Government should have done before he brought in these measures?
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), the present Chairman of the Finance Committee, was equally critical in a speech he made in the House on March 22, 1982. On April 5, 1982, the now Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) had this to say:
In fact, the Minister of Finance has been dragging us through the mill in the past few months and the provinces are, as it were, squirming in a financial strait-strait-jacket, because the federal Government is reducing its deficit by cutting funds to the provinces.
That is exactly what that gang over there is doing today. They are doing what they were so critical of when the Liberals tried to do it in 1982.
I could go on. The Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) and the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) were equally critical. The present Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) decried the cut-backs and predicted that the Atlantic provinces are singularly vulnerable to any federal Government belt-tightening in these areas. He said that on April 5, 1982.
You will be interested to hear, Mr. Speaker, that on February 7, 1984, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) said the following:
Mr. Speaker, this is a deplorable piece of legislation because the principle of it is one of betrayal. The Bill betrays the provinces of Canada, the provincial governments of Canada and betrays the universities of Canada. It betrays postsecondary institutions of Canada. It betrays the young people of Canada and it illustrates rank hypocrisy in the actions of the Government.
I have yet to hear him say that of today's Government because he is a part of it. Yet it is equally hypocritical for this Government to do what it accused the previous Government of doing.
The words of the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) were dandy when she spoke in the House on April 5, 1984. She castigated the Government for its inhumane treatment of and attitude toward Canada's sick. She deplored the fact that young people would be faced with huge increases in tuition fees in order to receive a higher education. In fact, she went on at great length to the point that the Liberal Government of the day was left practically without any credit at all.
I could go on, but I am quite sure that those who are interested may go through those speeches themselves and try to figure out the difference between that gang over there and the Liberal Government that was rejected by the Canadian people. There ain't any difference. In fact, if anything, this Government is more hypocritical than the previous one because of the criticisms it levelled at the previous Government for doing exactly what it is doing today. In fact, the cuts this Government is proposing are even more severe than those made by the Liberal Government.
I could go on and on about the impact of those cuts, but the real impact will be on the future of medicare. As a party that fought for everyone's right to adequate health care, we deplore

May 5, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
what the Government is doing. I want to address health care from another point of view, and that is, from the point of view of prevention.
I noticed that the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), in a speech he made last weekend to a conference, spoke about the need to bring in preventive health care programs for Canada's elderly. He waxed eloquent about preventive health care. He seemed to be sincere in what he was saying. The Minister of National Health and Welfare should stand in the House, be honest and criticize the Government for what it is doing to the programs under his Department. He should fight on behalf of the people of Canada and say that they have a right to adequate, good health care services, whether they live in Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Ontario, the prairie provinces, or indeed British Columbia. We have not heard a peep from him on the health care programs or on where we are going in the future development of health care.
If the Government gets away with what it is trying to do today, there will not be any health care about which to worry in the future because it will have effectively destroyed the entire medicare system in Canada.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the legislation before the House this afternoon. As we heard since this morning and last Friday, the Opposition has been giving the impression that the Members from Quebec are a bunch of spineless nobodies who could not care less about the interests of Quebec, and there were others who claimed that this legislation was going to deal a mortal blow to the finances of the Government of Quebec. We have been accused of the most heinous motives with respect to education and health care. We have supposedly become a bunch of sadists who are chortling with glee at the cutbacks in health care programs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: You are right.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I see some Members of the Opposition who are making petty politics out of this issue and who seem to think they will hoodwink Canadians and have them believe we are inconsistent, quite stupid and devoid of social conscience. They do not shy from attacking our Quebec Ministers by saying that they are not extremely quiet about this.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the truth is quite different. The truth is quite different because Quebec is also part of Canada; under the Civil Code provisions one is free to accept or reject a bankrupt inheritance, but there is no such option in politics. We have been saddled with the Liberal inheritance, our inheritance from all Canadian Liberals, and that is what we have to administer.
As a province Quebec must also accept its inheritance, and we were left with a deficit running into billions of dollars.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, here is what editorialist Michel Roy wrote in La Presse of March 11, 1985, and I quote:
There is no doubt that the equalization system set up under federal legislation on fiscal agreements is being severely tried this year. When the current agreements (1982-87) were negotiated in 1981-the central Government did everything it could to lighten the heavy burden of transfers to the provinces.
At the time-1981-82-the Liberals were in the driver's seat and they could see the balloon swelling, about to blow up any minute.
Michel Roy went on to say:
Because it was increasing at an amazing rate while compounding the deadlock of the federal deficit which now reaches the $35 billion mark, the decision was made to set a ceiling on the costs of established programs and to change the equalization formula-which profits six provinces-to the extent that the latter lost their guaranteed fiscal revenues which until then was their insurance that they would never in any year get an amount lower than the previous year's.
Since that new provision met with violent protests-
Of course, each province was interested in getting as much as possible from the federal Government
-Ottawa had agreed to extend to March 31st, 1985, the fiscal revenue guarantee. This means the provinces have known for three years that they would not get for fiscal year 1985-86 the amounts they had been expecting.
That decision was not taken by Mr. Mulroney. And it is no surprise to Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Opposition is playing petty politics with the Bill. Faced with such an inflation in the cost of social programs, the runaway increase of all transfer payments to the provinces, we took the opposite course from that followed by the Liberal Opposition when they were in power-we decided to restore some sort of order and to limit to 5 per cent the runaway increase of those costs, so that the provinces themselves would strive for a better management of their expenditures, make an in-depth review of their projects, and their programs. In so doing we invited them to duplicate this Government's collective effort to put to better use our expenditures and fiscal revenues. As you know, in all cases the Government is financing those programs often on a 50 per cent basis, but it has nothing to say about how the funds that are transferred to the provinces and to Quebec are spent. One does not need to have great divining powers to find out that it often happens that the provinces have used those funds for all sorts of purposes and for their miscellaneous expenditures. Nonetheless, as the central Government we have almost nothing to say.
Moreover, contrary to what the Opposition is now suggesting, we are actually reducing the runaway transfer costs. In absolute terms, they will not lose a penny. On the contrary, during the years to come, under those programs, the provinces will get additional funds of $25 billion.
Of course, we set a ceiling on the increase, we are asking the provinces to strive seriously for a rationalization of their expenditures. As a Quebecer and as a Canadian, as Members of the Quebec caucus, we have been following that exercise

May 5, 1986
and the consideration of the Bill. We could have allowed those costs to become inflated as the Liberals did. I think that on the whole, the Tory caucus agrees that such a step, far from axing those programs will allow a slower and more reasonable increase.
Mr. Speaker, this Government believes that this Bill is to the advantage both of the Government and of Canadian men and women of this and future generations, and we hope, because of this legislation, to be better able in coming months and years to meet their needs because we shall have at our disposal more substantial sources of financing and a reasonable budget which will take into our actual capacity to pay as a nation. Mr. Speaker, this is what this Bill proposes, it proposes common sense, logic and reason.
1 am sure that Canadians and Quebecers will not be fooled by the political games which are being played in this place to suggest that this Government is ignoring their concerns. That is not true. We do address their concerns and we shall continue to do so rationally, intelligently and with determination.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) because he said that the Opposition was engaging in petty politics in that it was upset about Bill C-96. Let us examine what the Member for Charlevois considers to be petty politics. Let us bear in mind that the Member's riding is located adjacent to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) and in between the Prime Minister's riding and Quebec City. Obviously being geographically close to the Prime Minister one could assume, given the importance of back-benchers in that administration, that this Member has the Prime Minister's ear and the Prime Minister has his ear. Indeed, he speaks straight from the horse's mouth, as it were, on behalf of the Prime Minister when he says that the Opposition's complaints about Bill C-96 are petty.
Let us see what petty matters the Opposition is complaining about. It is complaining about a cut in funds to the Province of Quebec in 1986-87 of $82.3 billion, a cut in 1987-88 of $174.9 million for education and health, another cut in 1988-89 of $277.2 million, a cut in 1989-90 of $389.2 million, a cut in 1990-91 of $512 million, and a cut in 1991-92 of $647.6 million, for a total petty cut to the Province of Quebec of $2,083.6 million. The Member for Charlevois, whose riding is geographically located next to the Prime Minister's and in between Quebec City thinks that that cut is petty. He has been listening to the Prime Minister. What are they saying in Quebec City?
The Minister of Finance for the Province of Quebec, who is in Quebec City and on the Member's other side and to whom the Member should sometimes listen, says that the measure is unfair to the provinces. You know what it is, Mr. Speaker? Let us call the federal Government the head of the household. This kind of financial measure, this kind of passing the deficit on to the provinces, is the equivalent of the head of the household buying himself a new suit, a new pair of shoes and showing his neighbours and friends how prosperous he is by wearing his new suit and shiny shoes, trying to convince his neighbours that he is prosperous because he dresses so well and has his finances in order. Meanwhile, other members of the family are pretty shabbily clothed, are ill fed and are doing without sufficient shelter. It is predatory prosperity that the Government is practising. The Government is saying to the people of Canada that because it has some magical mythical policy to reduce the deficit, it has passed $8 billion worth of deficit on to Canada's 10 provinces.
The federal Government, with its new suit on, says, "Look at that. We have our financial house in order", but the provinces, in so far as education and health is concerned, will be more shabbily dressed than ever. As a matter of fact, when you examine what is now happening in some of our postsecondary educational institutions and hospitals, let us say it is not an exaggeration to suggest that some of our provinces in those two fields will be naked, not just shabbily dressed.

May 5, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
I rise today to support this motion to apply a six-month hoist to Bill C-96. I have just come from a conversation in the last few minutes with a gentleman from the Newfoundland Legislature who is concerned about education in Newfoundland. He told me that in Memorial University in Newfoundland the average wage of faculty members is $8,000 below the wage paid in other Atlantic institutions. He told me that Memorial University has become a raiding institution for other colleges, not colleges that promise fantastic bonuses or additional perks but colleges that are simply offering a decent wage. He told me that 62 people this week are being laid off at Memorial University, that the Memorial extension program, which is setting up extension programs around our rather large province of Newfoundland and Labrador to bring the services of that university to people no matter where they live, is being cut. He told me that 30 people have been laid off in the medical institution in the last few months and that the Established Programs Financing as outlined in Bill C-96 will deliver a death-like blow to an institution that is already on its knees.
I have picked up Bill C-96 and have found out what it promises the Province of Newfoundland, a province that has the lowest per capita income in Canada, a province that has the highest per capita debt in the country. What do I see, Mr. Speaker? I see that $187.7 million is to be chopped in transfer payments to a province where the university is already disintegrating before our eyes and where health care and the days of getting reasonably good health care are nothing more than a fond memory.
That is not what Canada is all about. That is not cooperative federalism. That is not in the words of the Prime Minister, a brand new day for Canada. That is cowardice, Mr. Speaker. This Government is so infected with its own rhetoric and so committed to fulfilling its own propaganda that rather than get its own house in order, cut back its own programs, admit that the world is not as simple as ABC to fix as the Conservatives suggest, the Government is cutting back $8 billion to the provinces, $2 billion to the Province of Quebec, which cut the Hon. Member for Charlevoix calls petty.
Parliamentarians should always remind themselves as they sit in this Chamber, sometimes rather empty with an echo coming back at you, that what we say and do here is not just for the benefit of parliamentarians in the Chamber, not just for the benefit of the few who come to watch from the galleries, but ultimately what we say and, more important, what we do here will be measured by the people of Canada. The eyes of the people of Canada are on us now. They are telling us that any time we walk away from the young people, any time we say that the human potential, that is this nation, can be measured purely in dollars and cents in a corrupt attempt to reduce the deficit, we have failed in our responsibility.
The true measure of any country is the way we treat our senior citizens and the way we treat our citizens. When we say with respect to our senior citizens that health care which they
need and have come to depend upon in their old age may no longer be there, and when we say to our young people that they are a resource we cannot afford to invest in, we have failed in our responsibility.
I urge all Members to vote to suspend Bill C-96 for a period of six months so that the Government opposite may realize that a breach of faith with our citizens is more than a petty complaint.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not help thinking as I listened to my good friend and colleague who just sat down how strange it is to be in politics. One cannot help but wonder at the changes which take place with the changes of position in the House of Commons. I am sure that my good friend and colleague has not personally changed his view. He probably castigated the previous Liberal administration as severely as he has castigated the Conservative administration when the Liberal Government was instituting the very thing with which we are faced today. I say sincerely that I do not doubt for a moment that he would be one of the few voices in the Liberal caucus, together with his seat-mate, who would have risen to say how inappropriate it was to reduce the level of increase in the transfer payments to the provinces. I find it a dilemma when daily I hear my friends in the Liberal Party criticizing their friends in the Conservative Party for the very things which they themselves were about to do or had already started to do before they lost the last election. I suppose I will get used to it in time, but I do confess that it is difficult.
Nevertheless, I do agree with the comments that were made. The points which were made are absolutely correct. The inappropriateness of the Government's action is clear to anyone who cares to take a moment or two to try to analyse the impact of the actions proposed. Along with a number of other things, it establishes in my mind what is wrong with the Government. It is not able to set its priorities properly. It does not seem capable of fully understanding the impact of its actions. The shift in the weight of transfer payments is as ill-conceived, inadequately analysed, and improperly explained as is the Government's move toward free trade. When added to all of the other actions taken by the Government, it amounts to a failure by the Government to come to grips with the reality that is Canada.
Many years ago this country made a commitment to the maintenance of a standard of health and education which would be applicable regardless of where one lived within the broad expanse of Canada. The country made a decision years ago that the have areas of the land would be prepared to share with those which had not, or had less. This kind of action undermines the very essence of that understanding. That is what is wrong with what is happening. It goes to the very core of the co-operative federalism which is the historic birthright of Canadians.
May 5, 1986

It is impossible to provide an adequate level of health care or an adequate level of post-secondary education without the federal Government, with its vastly greater taxing powers, contributing proportionately to its capacity. That will not happen and will, therefore, result in the deterioration of the health care systems and post-secondary education systems which exist across the country. It is easy to say that either the provinces will take up the slack or individuals will be asked to pay some form of user-fee, which seems to be becoming the watchword for everything the Conservative Government does.
It is easy to say that, but when you ask people anywhere in Canada whether they will be able to provide for their children the monies necessary to allow them to continue with their education to the post-secondary level, the answer is inevitably that they are not able to do that any more. They say that their disposable income has been shrunk considerably by the federal Government, along with other Governments, taxing them to the point where they are unable to provide their families with that opportunity which is the basis for the greatness which Canada was in fact achieving. That happens to every family. I really wonder what the outcome of this action will be.
David Peterson, the Premier of Ontario, who is not exactly a soul mate of mine, in responding to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) at the First Ministers' Conference in November, said:
We are also dismayed by the federal Government's plans to cut Established Program Funding transfer payments for post-secondary education and health. These cuts will amount to about $6 billion over the next Five years. These cuts, which were announced without consultation, speeded up by a year without discussion, will weaken our country in the very areas where we must marshal our greatest strength-
In the fiscal year 1986-87 the Province of Ontario will receive $114 million less than it would have otherwise received. In the fiscal year 1987-88 it will receive $243 million less than it would otherwise have received. In 1988-89 it will receive $387.6 million less than it would otherwise have received. In 1989-90 it will receive $546.6 million less than it would otherwise have received. In 1990-91, at the end of the agreement, it will receive $722.7 million less than it would have otherwise received, for a total loss to the Province of Ontario of $2,014.1 million.
Given that post-secondary education and health are already under-funded, where will we get the money to maintain the standards which now exist, which in fact are even lower than the standards we had previously? We do not have sufficient funds to provide the opportunity for those who are in need of health care to go to a hospital and be made well, or for those young people upon whose brains the country will be built to continue their education in order to make Canada a stronger place. The Government had better re-think and re-establish its priorities. Right now it is destroying the co-operative federalism on which the country was built.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to the debate on Bill C-96, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977. We are presently speaking on a motion for a six-month hoist. I certainly agree that this Bill should be given a six-month hoist and brought back to the House with major changes because it is going to cause a lot of problems for the people of the country.
As the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) so eloquently put it, this country has had federal and provincial arrangements and collective agreements for many, many years. We have to maintain the right of all Canadians to equal access to quality health care and education no matter where they live. This Bill will cut $8 billion from the provinces by the year 1992. That money will have to come from the provincial Treasuries. Where are they going to get it? They get it from the same source as the federal Government here in Ottawa, namely, the taxpayer. In education, for example, if the provinces choose not to rely entirely on increased taxes to cover this shortfall, they could use another form of tax by increasing tuition fees. We already have many students, certainly in Atlantic Canada, who are having terrible difficulty in meeting the tuition fees they have to pay now. There are areas of this country, including my own province, where we have very high unemployment and very little opportunity for young people to find summer jobs in order to help finance their education. There are also economic circumstances in many places which work against the parents of those students being able to help financially. I am sure that any farmer in P.E.I. over this last year or so would have great difficulty in finding extra money to help his son or daughter to go to university. They, too, are in a serious financial bind.
We have heard it said in this debate today that this $8 billion cut-back is a transfer of the tax burden and deficit to the provinces. That, I submit, is the case. While the federal Government may be able to look good by reducing its deficit, it does not give relief to the ordinary citizen of this country because he or she is going to have to bear the burden of provincial taxation. These cuts will mean an accumulated loss, if you will, of $2,929 million from 1986 to 1992 for the Province of Ontario.
For my own Province of Prince Edward Island it will mean $1.6 million less for the year 1986-1987, $3.4 million for the year 1987-1988, $5.4 million for 1988-1989, $7.6 million for 1989-1990, $10 million for 1990-1991, and $12.7 million for 1991-1992. That is an accumulated loss, if you will, of $40.8 million. That represents well over $330 for every man, woman and child living in my province. Call it what you like, it is still a form of taxation because they are going to have to come up with that money which, in most cases, they just do not have. Someone is going to suffer.
What can the provinces do if they decide not to increase taxes? Should they cut the number of hospital beds? In my province there is a great need for an increase in health care, not a cut. What about education? Should the provinces close

May 5, 1986
Federal- Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
universities? My province has only one university, the University of Prince Edward Island. I do not think it would be a very wise decision for the Government to cut funding and close that university, especially at a time when the new veterinary college will be opening in the fall. Where is the money coming from for that? The educational system in my province is already financially strapped. Tuition fees are too high. University professors are working for less than the national average salary for their position. In these circumstances it is very difficult to find areas to make cuts in the so-called fat we hear so much of these days. Over the last number of years the Commission for Higher Education in Atlantic Canada has cut that fat to the bare bone, almost to the point where our educational system in Atlantic Canada is suffering. It is impossible to find more dollars there.
What about health care for our senior citizens? Of course, health care costs are increasing drastically. Yet how we treat our elderly is a measure of the kind of country we are. This Bill certainly flies in the face of what I have always thought Canada was all about; a place where we provide not only equal opportunity for education, but equal opportunity for quality health care to the best of our ability, no matter where you live. Obviously you cannot have everywhere the kind of hospital facilities that we have in, say, downtown Toronto. However, that is not to say we should not provide quality health care for our citizens. No matter whether they live in the north, or the extremities of the east or west, no matter whether they live anywhere in Ontario and Quebec, they should have equal opportunity to quality health care. However, when we look at provinces like Quebec and Ontario, we find a tremendous burden is going to be placed on some of our larger provinces. There will be cuts in service or tax increases.
Why is the Government doing this? It says it has to control the deficit. The Government brought in Bills which were debated and passed by this House to support the banks when they were in financial difficulty. We have supported the agricultural industry in the west. Certainly it needs the help, and certainly more money is needed to help farmers all across this country.
Let us not forget our young people. They are the future of our country, the ones who will be carrying on in the future. They are the men and women who will represent us in this astute Parliament and will be performing the functions of government. We should give them the opportunity to do the very best job possible. speechtext:

expenditures needed for health care and post-secondary education in this country.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) quoted at length Conservative Members presently in the Government and in the Cabinet. They railed against the Liberals from 1977 to 1984, except for a brief time in 1979, for what the Liberals were doing regarding funding for health care and post-secondary education. I think the Conservatives at that time were right. Then he had to sit and suffer while listening to Liberals making the same speech as the Tories did since 1977. I have been here a little longer than he has and have had to suffer through that as well.
I want to disagree with my colleague, because after quoting the Conservatives now in the government he concluded that "there ain't no difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives". Well, I disagree with him. There is one difference, and that is that one is in and one is out.
As Tommy Douglas said on more than one occasion, they take money from the rich and votes from the poor and then promise to protect them from each other. Nothing has changed between the Liberals and the Tories since the days of the "dirty thirties" when the Liberal Finance Minister said, "What do you think, money grows on gooseberry bushes?" They talked exactly the same way in the seventies and the eighties.
Something of which I am very proud is that my province, during the past four decades, led Canada and all of North America in health care, in the way we treat our sick and our old, and what we provide for our young by way of advanced education.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) just made the point that there is something wrong with the priorities of this Government and the previous one. He is dead on. Saskatchewan will lose $227.4 million between now and 1990-91. That is not a lot compared to Ontario, Quebec or even B.C. That is as much or more than one of those fighter planes. I was reminded of that by my colleague from Hamilton Mountain. The priority is always there on a fighter plane we neither need nor can use, instead of giving priority to those who are sick and need the fullest opportunity for secondary education.
This is the time to be expanding health care, educational facilities and opportunities, not reducing them. We readily agree that there has to be efficient spending, administration and delivery of federal funds through the provinces for the purposes of health care and post-secondary education, a better distribution of medical practitioners, which should mean additional costs to be shared equally by the federal Government with the provinces. There should be specialists in outlying areas of our provinces and our territories who should be paid additional money.
There should be the latest technology available in some of our outlying areas to allow the best medical practitioners to treat people as equally, in terms of medical practice, as they
May 5, 1986

would in downtown Toronto or downtown Regina. That means higher cost, and I have yet to run into any taxpayer in Canada of any political stripe who is not willing and prepared to pay his or her fair and equitable share of taxes to do that very thing.
We should provide opportunities for people to pursue secondary education and quit becoming a nation of exploited hamburger slingers, gas pump jockeys, bellhops, sky caps and taxi drivers. In fact, I ran into a taxi driver last week with a masters degree. They are all exploited for the benefit of what is called free and open market forces. Their talents are wasted. The priorities of this Government are banks, before farmers and home owners. The priority of this Government is its paranoia and hysteria about deficits, before farmers, fishermen, and, more seriously, before the poor, the old, the sick and those who try to pursue excellence in education.
An Hon. Member spoke last Friday and said that, "We can only provide what we can afford to pay". He proceeded to go on and on about our debt. After all those decades of fighting we finally arrived at a 50/50 partnership between the national Government, the provinces and the Territories. The onus is on the federal Government to say to the provinces, "We will share with you 50/50 improvements and expansion in health care and postsecondary education". I want to close by quoting one of my favourite political heroes and mentors. Mr. Douglas, at our convention in Regina in 1983, during one of his most famous speeches, said, after all these years of fighting and gains: "Don't let them take it away". I believe he was being relatively non-partisan.

We will go to whatever lengths we must, under the law and parliamentary procedure, to persuade the Government not to continue doing what the Liberals began.
The people of Canada are willing to pay and are willing to share with one another, from coast to coast, in what we need, what we support and what we must do over the next number of years to keep our nation in the forefront and show others how we can be a decent and civilized society for everyone in our country.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret having only 10 minutes to talk about this very important betrayal by the federal Government of its traditional responsibilities to the provinces. That betrayal is particularly unseemly for a Government that campaigned on the promise
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
that there would be new and good relations between the central Government and the provinces-changes for the better once the so-called days of confrontation were put behind them.
In speaking to this budget Bill, I want to focus on an even more significant question. It is the important promises that were made during the election campaign that the new Conservative Government would save the Canadian taxpayers billions of dollars by terminating the waste and extravagance of the former Trudeau Government. After campaigning on the promise that it would be possible to reduce the cost of Government by billions of dollars, without cutting important programs, let us consider where the billions of dollars are being cut from federal government waste and extravagance.
The first point to be made about the billions of dollars being cut is that they are a measure of proof that the Government has not found the billions of dollars in waste and extravagance. Surely even a Conservative Government, with a philosophy that there should be less Government and that the provinces should be allowed to function themselves and finance programs in their own areas of responsibility, would not cut these postsecondary and health care programs if it could have kept its promise to cut the waste and extravagance that it had identified for the Canadian people.
The Government has cut the Established Programs Financing, which is the national Government's way of supporting post-secondary education and health care. I have a chart to which some of my colleagues have referred. It shows that if this Bill goes through, there will be a cut across the country of $317.4 million in 1986-87 in money that would otherwise be given to the provinces for those two very important purposes. In 1987-88, the cut-back will amount to $676.8 million, slightly over $1 billion in 1988-89, and $1.5 billion in 1989-90. In 1990-91, the cut for that year alone is slightly over $2 billion, and in 1991-92, six years from now, the cut will be $2.5 billion if this Bill is passed. The total for that entire period is slightly over $8 billion.
While the Budget has succeeded in saving the federal Government slightly over $8 billion, that saving has not come from cutting waste and extravagance or tightening the federal Government's belt in its areas of discretionary spending. That savings was not achieved by cutting back the size of the Public Service or locating the waste and extravagance about which the Government campaigned and which it tried to pin on the Trudeau Government. It comes as a result of asking the provinces to tighten their belts and deprive Canadians across Canada of support for two of the most important social programs-post-secondary education and health care.
I want to look at the situation in my Province of Ontario. The proposed cut for 1986-87 would be $114 million; nearly $250 million in 1987-88; almost $400 million in 1988-89; over $500 million in 1989-90; nearly $750 million for 1990-91; and $916 million in 1991-92. That is a total of almost $3 billion over that six-year period.

May 5, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
The federal Government and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) have been asked to acknowledge at least these figures which come from their own documents. I suppose they are hoping that the Canadian people will not listen to what these figures suggest so that the Government will not have to defend the facts contained herein. When asked if these figures are true, the junior Minister of Finance has repeatedly refused to face up to them but simply stated that each year the Government will be paying more to the provinces than the previous year.
The Government cannot deny the fact that if this Bill is passed there will be a reduction by the amounts I have cited as compared to what the provinces would get if this Bill does not pass.
1 suggest that the Government has underestimated the Canadian people. They are not so stupid as to believe that simply because the amounts to be paid to the provinces will increase a little every year, they are not being cut back by the amounts we have suggested from the Government's figures. The provinces are being asked to tighten their belts by somewhat over $8 billion over a six-year period.
The federal Government has been a partner in these two programs since their creation. I recall in 1967 how much the federal Government pushed to bring all the provinces on board in order to establish medicare. It is true that medicare is within provincial jurisdiction, but the federal Government backed that program. In effect, we told the provinces that if they passed that legislation we would support these programs. The purpose of the legislation was to support these programs.
The federal Government promised Canadians that it would cut back the cost of Government, but instead of cutting back on the cost of the federal Government it is cutting back and asking for belt-tightening on behalf of provincial Governments.
I want to ask the Government a number of questions about health care. Should the provincial Government of my province, Ontario, respond to the federal Government's reduced support by cutting the number of hospital beds? Should it cut the number of emergency departments in hospitals? Should it cut out health care for senior citizens? Should it cut out the tremendous support which has been given to cancer research? Should hospitals be closed? Should we force our senior citizens or the handicapped in Ontario and elsewhere in the country to pay user-fees? With this great leadership which it is showing in cutting back expenditures, how does the Government expect the provinces to respond to the cut-backs in health care?
I know that I have but a minute left. Yet I have more questions. I think the Government owes something to Canadians if it is withdrawing support and no longer wants to be an equal partner in university and post-secondary education. How does the Government expect the provinces to respond to this series of enormous cuts? Should universities be closed? Should research at universities be terminated? Should we close our
professional, medical, dental, business and architecture schools? Should we close computer and high technology departments at universities? And what about agriculture and research programs at universities? Should we increase tuition fees?
What really revolts us is when we hear the federal Government responding to such questions with a new discovery. It has discovered waste and extravagance in these programs. In order to get elected the Government convinced the public that it would cut waste and extravagance in the federal Government. Now that the Government is in place and finds that there is not waste and extravagance, it proposes to cut funding of health care and post-secondary education. Members of the Government say that these areas can be cut easily because there is a great deal of waste and extravagance in them. That allegation is just a lot of nonsense.
I urge Members of the House, even Conservative Members, to vote against this nefarious piece of legislation.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), I feel obligated-not pleased, but obligated-to participate in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-96. This Bill is basically legislation to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act.
As Hon. Members have pointed out before me, the thrust of this important piece of legislation is simply to cut back on two crucial and national areas of importance, that is, education and health. Basically, there is a feeling within Canada that the Government is tranferring its responsibility with respect to what it says and preaches in terms of deficit reduction to the provinces.
What will this mean in the Province of Ontario? What will it mean to the people of Ontario? This year it will mean a reduction of some $114 million. Following the statistics and numbers through preceding years, it will result in a loss of some $2,929 billion-almost $3 billion-in direct losses alone between the years 1986 and 1992 in the Province of Ontario. The Premier of Ontario, Mr. David Peterson, said:
You don't call it a cut. You could call it a breach of faith-You have not solved the National problem . . . You are only transferring that National problem to us.
The Treasurer of Ontario, Mr. Robert Nixon, said:
There was uniform opposition to Ottawa's plan . .. Nobody thought it was a good idea.
I could go on and quote various provincial Ministers and Premiers who are basically and philosophically opposed to this move. However, I will not.
As a federal Member of Parliament I think this piece of legislation and the cuts we are seeing in the areas of health and education really assist in defining what it means to be a Conservative in this Government and in this country. It really defines, on philosophical grounds, where the Government is coming from and where it wishes to go. I think we can measure
May 5, 1986

how progressive and compassionate a society is when we measure how it treats its sick, elderly and its future resources, namely, youth.
In talking about cut-backs let me say that there are a great many Canadians who hope that their Governments will be prudent in terms of spending their tax dollars. In the end, our primary responsibility here in this Chamber is to ensure that the monies collected from Canadians are properly channelled and used in a fiscally responsible manner. However, when one talks to average Canadians, as I have done in my own constituency and across the country, one finds that two areas in which they are not prepared to sacrifice are the very areas in which the Government proposes to cut back. There is health on the one hand and education on the other. In dealing with these two subjects we see an indication of how the Government is treating its seniors, its sick and its disabled on the one hand and, on the other, how it treats its young people vis-d-vis their education.
We have heard in the Chamber speech after speech stating that medicare is a tribute to its great traditions. We have heard about how important it is to support technological training and to educate our young people. It is not important for every Canadian to come out of school with a BA, an MA or a PhD from one of the local universities, but it is important that there be no stigma attached to the individual who wishes to pursue academic excellence vis-a-vis college and come out with a trade of which he or she can be proud.
We are talking about crucial elements here today. In Ontario, we will not have $3 billion at our disposal to ensure that the level of medical health care enjoyed in our province throughout the years will be maintained. In Ontario, we will have $3 billion less to secure better education and, therefore, a better future for our young citizens. They may be young today but, God willing, tomorrow they will be our leaders, whether it be in the business community, the social service community or in the politcal community. When we talk about robbing billions and billions of dollars from our provincial Governments, we are talking about a serious, fundamental matter which goes to the core of what our country is all about.
If the Government were to say that it is cutting back because it is supposed to cut back, then obviously that would be a constitutional issue. Citizens would at least be reassured that those monies would be channelled in those directions in the end. When we have citizens who will not be able to enjoy those funds in terms of health care or education then they are not pleased. This is why we are rising in our places today to demonstrate and articulate these concerns. We are doing so in order to make the Government aware of these aspirations in the eleventh hour.
We should not consider this piece of legislation in isolation. I think it puts forward a continuity with respect to programs and policies which demonstrate just where the interests of the Government lie. It is prepared to bail out the banks, no questions asked. It is prepared to come to the House and say to members of the Opposition: "You sign a blank cheque. Don't
Federal- Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
worry about it. We know how to deal with it". Yet in the same breath it comes before the House and tries to deindex the pensions of senior citizens. The Government is prepared to give a capital gains bonanza of $500,000, yet it is prepared to deindex baby bonuses. It is prepared to ask those who earn $200,000 annually to pay a cumulative tax of only 2 per cent in five years while asking those who earn $15,000 annually to face a 36 per cent increase in taxes by 1990.
After illustrating those individual cases and analysing the philosophical bent that characterizes these policy thrusts, it comes as no surprise that the Government is asking for, and will obtain because of its majority, cuts to health care and post-secondary education that will have a tremendous impact. In speech after speech, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has talked about today's youth, tomorrow's leaders, today's ill and tomorrow's old. If there is any sincerity and integrity in those words, those press releases and those policy statements, then the Government will withdraw Bill C-96 because the legislation is immoral. It lacks integrity and it lacks the vision and compassion necessary to protect Canadians through health care and post-secondary education services. Canadians know where the Government is going. It is important, however, that the Government learn where Canadians are going to go in 1988.

However, a taxpayer who has the honour and the privilege of having an annual income of around $100,000, will pay only 1 per cent more income tax. This means that the Conservative Government's measures to reduce the deficit are putting the greatest burden on those who are already being squeezed and giving a better chance to those who are already well-off.
This Government, which in its frenzy to reduce the deficit is bearing down most heavily on low-income Canadians, is doing

So, Mr. Speaker, the provinces unanimously condemned and denounced these unfair cutbacks, particularly because they were made without real consultation, as the provinces point out. I do not really expect the Government to take my word for it. I am going to quote the Quebec Minister of Finance, the province I represent here in the House. Mr. Speaker, this was published in the Journal de Montreal of May 2, barely three days ago:
Last night Quebec Finance Minister Gerard D. Levesque accused the Canadian Government of unilaterally-
-unilaterally. It proves what I just said, there was no real consultation. As he was saying:
-of unilaterally changing the provincial Fiscal transfer mechanisms.
And I quote the minister directly:
It is like a vice closing progressively on the public finances of Quebec- "another step toward a federal withdrawal from the financing of essential services-
This is how a provincial Finance Minister has reacted to this Bill, and he was the first to say that this Bill was imposed unilaterally. Mr. Speaker, it is to this that we object the most, because this measure is not only hard, but it is also being imposed on the provinces without their consent.
How will the provinces react to such substantial cutbacks in their finances? I have the impression that their only option will be to reduce their services.
How can this be done in the case of hospital services? As we know, certain provinces have been looking at user-fees for some time, and several of them will probably have to charge user-fees to make up for the shortfall of $8 billion during the next six years, and these additional costs will be charged to people whose taxes have just been substantially increased by $12.5 billion over two years, as I said earlier. If the provinces do not charge user-fees, what will they do? In some cases, they will
certainly postpone the purchase of new equipment, such as modern X-ray machines or other things they may need.
Elsewhere, the number of beds available in hospitals may have to be reduced because of the cutbacks forced on the hospitals by the provinces when they transfer the costs imposed on them by the federal Government, or else it might be the lineups in the emergency rooms which will grow longer. Of course, emergency room line-ups are already quite long enough without them growing any longer, at least in my own province. For my part, I maintain that the cutbacks of $2 billion which Quebec will have to absord within a few years can only cause further deterioration of hospital services in our province.
Moreover, what I find strange is that this remedy is being administered by a political party which was saying just the opposite not so long ago. You must recall, Mr. Speaker, the famous Sherbrooke caucus held shortly before the 1984 federal elections. That was already a very well known caucus meeting. For instance, it was the caucus meeting during which the Conservative Party promised to maintain indexation of Old Age Security pensions. Let me recall what came afterwards, when the Minister of Finance came up with proposals to do the exact opposite, proposals that were aimed at deindexing Old Age Security pensions. And we know that senior citizens all across Canada were forced to rise and organize demonstrations right up to Parliament Hill, asking the Conservative Party and the present Prime Minister to honour their commitment.
Well, concerning financial support to hospital services, let me refer for instance to one of the commitments made in Sherbrooke by the Conservative Members' caucus. In addition to maintaining Old Age Security pensions, they were committed to honouring the federal obligation-this is how they called it, the obligation-to support provincial health care services and to provide extra funds. Not a word was said about cuts at that point. They talked about increasing the payments that would be transferred to the provinces.
How hard it does seem to the Conservative Party to be true to their word once they have promised something!
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me make a few comments-I know I have some time left-on another area where cuts will hurt very badly. I am referring to post-secondary education. I must comment on that, because in my constituency I have three universities: McGill University, Concordia University and the Universite du Quebec a Montreal. There is no need then to talk about the number of representations I received against Bill C-96. At a point in time where we speak of the importance of education in a technological society, the urgent need to improve our competitive position, especially in the face of free trade and negotiations with the United States, how does the Government expect to reach its goals if it cuts down on the funds intended for college and university education? It makes no sense, Mr. Speaker. That is not the place where to make cuts, at a time when students have difficulty finding summer jobs to pay for their education, at a point where parents have
May 5, 1986

already their available income reduced by increased taxes, because they will then be forcing universities to increase tuition fees. Thousands of students in my constituency are especially concerned about that. They ask me to point out to Parliament that it is not the proper time to increase school fees because many of them with slender means will thus be unable to attend university.
If I had more time at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I could carry on, but since I have only a few minutes left, I should like to explain to Canadians through you why I will be unable to vote for Bill C-96.

-respect the federal obligation to fund provincial health care through Established Programs Financing, and make additional funds available to the provinces on a cost-shared basis for the establishment or enrichment of programs deemed most likely to improve the general level and limit long-term costs. This determination to be made following a national conference of health Ministers and health care professionals.
It is obvious through this legislation that the Conservative Government has not kept that promise. The Conservative Party committed itself to increase R and D expenditures to 2.5 per cent of GNP as compared to 1.17 per cent in 1981. The Conservative Party said:
Our research and development commitment is fundamental to our over-all programs for economic and social development. We are committed to doubling Canada's R and D budget to 2.5 per cent of GNP.
The Conservative Government has already broken that promise through cut-backs as a result of the last two Budgets. The Government is underscoring the way it broke that promise through cut-backs in support for universities as a result of this bad piece of legislation.
Again I say, what is new about another broken Conservative promise? There have been so many already, but this is one of the most serious. Through this legislation Conservatives are hitting health care, something fundamental to this country. They are also hitting education, something fundamental to this country. They are imposing permanent damage on the country and the people. This bad Bill must be defeated, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to deal with this Bill, not with much pleasure, but in order to put on the official record of our debates in the House some opinions and views that I would like to elaborate on.
Because the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) who has spoken before me has provided a fairly complete overview of the facts, I shall refrain from repeating the arguments he has put forward, namely, that the Government has failed to consult the provinces before making its decision, that under the circumstances it is acting not only arbitrarily, but also with a complete lack of sensitivity for the greatest needs of today, namely, education and health care.
I wish to indicate simply that I support the views of my colleague, that we will vote against this Bill and that, when the time comes, we will stand up against this initiative aimed at considerably reducing the amounts of money which the provinces expected and were entitled to receive.
Mr. Speaker, the Government proposes to reduce the growth rate of its contribution to Established Programs Financing. The total reduction in cash transfers and fiscal percentage points could amount to about S8.133 billion for Canada as a whole.
For my own province of Ontario, it will be almost $3 billion, more precisely $2,929 billion. We cannot help wondering where the provincial Governments will find the money to finance their essential programs in the areas of health and education. In fact, as a result of these cutbacks, the provinces will either have to raise their taxes or increase their deficit, and give us the same lame excuse this Government has given us, namely that they have to do it to reduce the deficit. Oh, the Government is doing it, if that is what it wants, but it is doing it at the expense of the provinces. It is doing it by tranferring the federal deficit to the provinces.
I think the whole procedure is less than fair and certainly does not meet with the approval of the general public.
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. colleague from Windsor West (Mr. Gray) said earlier, this Government has acted without consulting the provinces and without their consent. It has failed to respect the tradition of federal-provincial arrangements, arrangements this Government had sworn to strengthen and abide by, while promising practically continuous consultation.
Mr. Speaker, we have here a striking example of a government that, as I said earlier, is insensitive to the needs of the provinces and has no scruples about breaking its word and then saying it is for the good of Canadians. This is a deficit that is going to be reduced to a federal deficit, as someone said earlier.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of debate I heard several Members of the New Democratic Party say that the Liberals did the same thing during the 6-and 5-period, and that we had cut payments for post-secondary education and education financing. It is true that during the 6-and 5-period, we cut financing for post-secondary education. And Hon. Members are aware that this represents about 27 or 28 per cent of total transfer payments to the provinces for health care and education, in other words, Established Programs Financing.
Mr. Speaker, the remaining 71 per cent relate to health programs. We should not forget that the 6-and-5 program was for only two years, whereas the thrust of Bill C-96 which is now under consideration will make the cutbacks permanent. It will have a very negative and severe impact on the future of our health and education services. We know that the number of college and university students has risen rather sharply this year. We know that the demand for hospital beds in Canada is on the increase. This week I wrote a letter in support of a request made by the Elisabeth-Bruyere health centre, a letter addressed to Sister Gilberte Paquette and dated April 29, not so long ago, in which I told her I had learned of her request with great interest. Mr. Speaker, it is a request for 70 additional nursing home beds. One thing we can readily appreciate in that respect is that we do not have French nursing care services here

in Ottawa, and I would suggest this is an altogether normal request from a well known health centre like Elisabeth-Bruyere. But what is happening, Mr. Speaker, is that because of these reduced payments to the provinces, particularly health services payments, the Elisabeth-Bruyere health centre is probably in a precarious position where it will not be getting the funds required to provide these 70 beds and serve people who urgently need financial assistance.
Mr. Speaker, under the old formula, the federal contribution for each province was equal to a yearly per capita amount indexed each year to the per capita Gross National Product multiplied by the population of the province. This is how we can evaluate the impact of Established Programs Financing.
The new legislation provides that this per capita amount will be indexed to the per capita GNP minus 2 p. 100.
This, Mr. Speaker, is where we do not agree with the Government, and we have said so many times, because it is unfair to do such a thing without consulting the provinces and without hearing the views of those concerned to find out the needs of the provinces and the users of these services.
Mr. Speaker, God knows that the Conservatives promised during the electoral campaign to keep to the Established Programs Financing Agreements, but this is just one of many broken promises. Whether we are speaking about pension indexing, Established Programs Financing or Government programs, everything has been left in suspense and it is impossible to know where we are going. This is a Government of indecision. This Government prefers to act alone. This Government acts before it consults. We have a Government which objects to certain things which I, at least, find essential in health care, because by objecting to a reasonable growth in Established Programs Financing, the Government is also objecting to an increase in the number of hospital beds, to improved post-secondary education and to reasonable and continuing access to these programs.
Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning, this Government is simply transferring its deficit to the provinces and the only reason it has given to justify this cutback is that all Canadians and all provinces must make an effort to reduce the federal deficit.
Mr. Speaker, as I have already said, and I shall close with this comment, the Government has acted unilaterally without the consent of the provinces and has not respected the tradition of federal-provincial agreements. We shall be voting against this Bill, Mr. Speaker, and we will resume this discussion in committee or when the Bill is in committee.

subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-PROVISION OF FIGHTER AIRCRAFT TO TURKEY-GREEK CYPRIOTS' FEARS
NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-PROVISION OF FIGHTER AIRCRAFT TO TURKEY-GREEK CYPRIOTS' FEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you well know, Canadians of Greek origin are extremely concerned about the fact that the Canadian Government intends to transfer CF-104 fighter aircraft to Turkey. It is bad enough from the perspective of Canadians of Greek origin that their former homeland was dominated and occupied for some 350 years by Turkey. It is bad enough that a few years ago the Defence Minister of Turkey quite openly indicated that Turkey claimed the Greek Aegean island as its own. It is bad enough that in 1974 some 40,000 Turkish troops invaded Cyprus and drove the Greek-Cypriot community into the southern part of the island. Since that time, thousands of Greek-Cypriots have been missing and unaccounted for.
As well, it is bad enough that Amnesty International continually condemns the activities of Turkey. It is bad enough that Turkey, as one of the NATO allies, has refused to take part in NATO exercises when Greece is involved. All of these things are bad enough.
On top of that, Canadians of Greek origin have invested their tax dollars in CF-104 fighter aircraft. This situation is somewhat akin to one which could have developed in 1939 if the Canadian Government of the time had decided to transfer military equipment to the Government of Nazi Germany on the verge of the German invasion of Europe. When one considers all of those things, I think it is understandable that Canadians of Greek origin are modestly upset, to say the least.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) has quite properly explained and pointed out that in 1976, all of the NATO countries, including Canada, Greece and Turkey, came to an agreement whereby surplus military equipment was to be transferred free of cost to Greece, to Turkey or to any other NATO ally if it was so requested. The Minister of National Defence explained as well that when Canada decided to replace its CF-104 fighter aircraft with new CF-18 aircraft, Canada offered its old fighter aircraft to all of its NATO allies and particularly to Turkey and Greece. The Minister pointed out as well that Turkey made a request to have those aircraft transferred, but Greece did not. He stated that later, Canada informed all of its allies of Turkey's claim to these aircraft and at that time, Greece made no response.
In 1982, after the offer had been made, Turkey had accepted it and Greece had not responded, the then Minister of National Defence under the former Liberal Government, the Hon. Gilles Lamontagne, made a commitment in principle to transfer the CF-104 aircraft to Turkey. Later, that commitment in principle was confirmed by another former Liberal Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Jean-Jacques Blais. Then in July 1982, for the very first time Greece requested the Canadian Government to transfer CF-104 aircraft and spare parts to it as well as to Turkey.
It was said by the present Minister of National Defence that we made a commitment to Greece at that time that we would transfer an equal amount of military equipment to Greece as was being transferred to Turkey and on the same terms as we were transferring it to Turkey. Those terms were that the equipment could not be used against another NATO ally and that it would be transferred in an "as-is" condition. There would not be any money spent to upgrade the equipment or improve it or do anything at all to make sure that it was in better condition when it was transferred than it was when it was being used by our own forces. On April 25 of this year, the Ottawa Citizen reported that the Department of National Defence was now combing its inventories for spare parts and for air frames for CF-104 aircraft to give to Greece in order to fulfil its commitment.
I would like to know tonight from the Parliamentary Secretary first to what extent we have now transferred CF-104 aircraft to Turkey and how many more remain untransferred to date. I would like to know from the Parliamentary Secretary whether any Canadian taxpayers' money was spent on upgrading those aircraft when they were transferred to Turkey. I would also like to know whether there is any
May 5, 1986

intention of spending any other Canadian taxpayers' dollars on upgrading those aircraft transferred to Turkey. I would like to know how much in the way of military equipment we have transferred so far to Greece in order to fulfil our commitment to Greece. As well, I would like to know exactly what kinds and how much additional military equipment we intend to transfer to Greece in order to fulfil our commitment to Greece subsequent to our commitment to Turkey.
Finally, I want to know from the Parliamentary Secretary if Canada has made a decision on whether or not we will be building a CANDU nuclear reactor for Turkey, whether or not the project will be proceeded with and, if it is, whether we intend to do something similar for Greece. I am looking forward to the answers of the Parliamentary Secretary tonight.
