AIR SAFETY-ARCTIC AIRPORTS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 25, I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) concerning the reinstatement of the Arctic airports program. The Minister's reply was sympathetic because it reflected the personal concern which I know him to have with regard to the matter. However, it was not a committal. I can understand that too because I know the financial constraints under which the Minister operates.
I should like to take this opportunity to argue again in favour of the reinstatement of the Arctic airports program. First I should like to quote from report No. 83-W30065 of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board which dealt with a fatality that took place at Paulatuk in the winter of 1983. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board has seen, as a result of investigating several aircraft accidents in the North with fatalities, that there is an underlying contributory cause. It found as follows:
The Board notes that many northern landing strips are rudimentary and have been developed with only local resources. In a 1978 Memorandum of Understanding between several federal Government Departments and the Governments of the Territories, standards for the identification and upgrading of northern aviation facilities were prescribed. The MOU expired in March 1983, at which time there were a number of facilities which had been identified as qualifying for upgrading or replacement, but for which implementation of the project had not been completed.
The report goes on:
The CASB is concerned that the inadequacy of aviation facilities at many Arctic community aerodromes may be compromising aviation safety in northern operations. Therefore, the Board is reviewing the circumstances from recent occurrences at such aerodromes with a view to possibly making formal recommendations regarding the requirement to re-identify substandard facilities and to develop a program to upgrade or replace any safety deficient facilities.
I would certainly encourage the Board to do just that. Just about everyone in the North is united that the program be completed because they share a common danger. They have to fly into these places. All three federally represented political Parties are in agreement. It does not matter whether it is the association of municipalities, the Chamber of Commerce or native organizations, they too are all of one mind. Several motions have been passed in the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories urging both the territorial and federal Governments to get their act together and reinstate this program.
The program was very successful during the period it was in operation. It was deeply appreciated by the people in various communities that now have good basic standard airstrips. You could think of places like Aklavik, Fort McPherson, Fort Norman and Fort Liard. It should be noted that some of these locations are on the road network, but there are other places sadly lacking in facilities and in need of proper upgrading.
Fort Franklin had a recent fatality and has been waiting for some time to get a proper airstrip. It is a community serviced exclusively by air. There is no road there at all. The airports at

May 5, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Rae Lakes and at Lac La Matre are in very poor shape. Something has to be done pretty quickly or we will have a Fort Franklin type disaster in the near future. Fort Good Hope is another example of a strip that needs to be upgraded.
My pitch today, Mr. Speaker, is that we get together, the federal Government, its various Departments-it might be Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Transport, Defence, anybody who is involved-and the territorial government. Let us have a concerted effort to finish the job that got cut off in mid stream in 1983. This would be a worthwhile use of public funds and do much to increase aviation safety in the part of Canada that I have the honour to represent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want you to know that we are very impressed by your versatility and clean-shavedness. In response to the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), I would like to say that we are all struck by his familiarity with the difficulties historically experienced by people who attempt to travel in the North. They constantly face dangers in attempting to go from place to place. Many of us who come from more densely populated areas, such as southwestern Ontario where my riding is, do not realize how many difficulties are faced by people in our northern communities. He has brought that concern forward very clearly.
As the Member mentioned, the program which Finished in 1983 expended between $65 million and $70 million up until that time. That program resulted in the completion of eight airports in Yukon and 30 airports in the Northwest Territories, which was a very major effort. Having done that, in March of 1983 nine communities remained isolated in terms of the criteria that were used to establish those other airports. That is not to say, however, that all funding had been stopped. Indeed, $10.6 million in additional funds have been spent through the operating and maintenance resources to upgrade facilities in many of those places. There has, therefore, been a significant contribution since September of 1984 in spite of the original program being terminated at the end of 1983.
1 will very quickly mention several other initiatives that have been undertaken which I think have contributed to safe air travel in the north. One of them is the weather improvement program which was funded by Transport Canada and continued to improve the quality of weather service in northern Canada. It is largely completed now and under that program, which will cost approximately $ 11 million, there is a CBC program dedicated to aviation weather broadcast each weekday morning. That may be one of the few non-biased CBC reports we get each day. As well, satellite weather photos are now available at Yellowknife, White Horse, Resolute Bay, Inuvik, and Frobisher Bay on a regular basis. In addition, Transport Canada, in conjunction with the Atmospheric Environment Service, is promoting the research and development of automatic weather reporting devices.
The program which the Member has asked to have reinstituted is now being reconsidered by the Minister, who is actively discussing it with his Cabinet colleagues. I am sure that he will be interested in the specific proposal suggested by the Member.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-PREOCCUPATION OF WOMEN CONCERNING SOCIAL PROGRAMS. (B) NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION
SOCIAL SECURITY-PREOCCUPATION OF WOMEN CONCERNING SOCIAL PROGRAMS. (B) NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which I want to pursue at this time is with regard to the review of social programs which the Conservative Government has undertaken, and particularly women's concerns with these programs. I am concerned about whether or not the review will be open, whether women's organizations will be consulted, and whether the review will include the possibility of improvement in the social programs rather than just cut-backs.
The response I received from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) was not very encouraging on this score. He made no mention as to the possibility of improvement in the social programs. One worries that "review" is simply a euphemism for "anticipated cut-backs". He certainly was in favour of openness. He said that the request for specific funding for women's organizations to take part in this review process would be given respectful consideration. However, he did not say anything stronger than that.
Since those remarks were made, other things have happened. Women's organizations have had a tougher time getting funding at all. In fact, major organizations have not received funding for this year, let alone extra funding to hire staff to prepare briefs and analyses in order to take part in the review process. We must worry about this participation. Women's organizations are getting some feedback from the Department which indicates that the review process will not be an open one, and they are extremely concerned about that.
I want to spend a few minutes specifically discussing funding for women's organizations. The idea that these organizations should have to present an application to the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) in order to lobby is something many organizations are very concerned about. There is no recognition of the fact that volunteer organizations are performing a vital role for Canada and they need and are entitled to this funding.
Volunteers do an enormous amount of work. Sometimes they are given far too much work to do and they need more, better and predictable funding. It might be too tempting for the Government to simply cut off the funding of these organizations. In the short run, it would be correct that these organizations would be quieter. They would not have the money to lobby. Ultimately, however, I think they would find ways to fight back.
May 5, 1986

We need better ways of funding these organizations. We have to recognize it as a matter of right and not use the state as an agency which receives applications and decides which organization will get money or not. The people should make this decision. This could be done as people fill out their tax returns. A special amount could be allocated to taxpayers, indeed to homemakers who are not taxpayers because we would certainly want all adult citizens included, so they can allocate a certain amount of their tax money to the voluntary sector to support the organizations they believe represent their interests. That would be a far better way of handling this, and we certainly want to see the amounts improved as well.
On the issue of social programs themselves, women's organizations and women in general have been strong advocates of a good social security system and universality. We should not be surprised by this because women are even more dependent than men for support on our universal programs at different times of their lives. By and large, women look after the health of the family. Women pick up the pieces when other members of the family have problems. The law of the jungle operates since it is women who have to tend to the wounded. They are much more sensitive to the need for well functioning health care, family allowance, child support and pension programs. Of course, women are much less likely to get private pensions and are therefore much more dependent on public pensions. In this respect, women are much less ideological and more practical than men. If the private sector is not doing the job, they are quite prepared to turn to the Government to see it done. They want action. In the matter of child care, the private sector has been abysmally lacking in the provision of adequate, quality, affordable child care. Women's organizations then turn to Government for action. They want their tax dollars devoted to this important matter of raising children adequately to see that they grow up well. Even in a time of restraint, they are very practical. They say this is a high priority for us and we want to see some action.
Social programs in Canada are not generous by international standards. Canada is ninth out of 12 among OECD countries in its support of social programs. A little less on pensions, I am sorry to say; but average in health and education, and above average on unemployment insurance. This is not because we are more generous in our benefits, but because we have so much unemployment. There has been an erosion in these programs. The family allowance used to pay more in real terms. The old age pension has been allowed to erode. Of course, unemployment insurance has been cut back. Women want to stop this erosion and see that the social security system meets current needs. This situation has developed because other priorities have been allowed to take over, things such as the funding of corporate giveaways.
Actual expenditures on universal social programs are not nearly as great as people think. For 1986-87, family allowance payments are estimated at $2.53 billion. Old age pensions cost $9.51 billion. Medicare costs $6.8 billion. The Government contribution to umemployment insurance is $2.68 billion. As
Adjournment Debate
well, the old age pension and family allowance are also taxed back. We are talking here about expenditures of $107 billion. Corporate give-aways are in the order of $30 billion to $50 billions.
The interest paid to Canadians who have enough money to loan to the Government on our public debt is in the order of $27 billion. The social programs are not taking up as much money as people think. It is a very serious mistake of the Government to suggest that we have to look to cut-backs in the social programs instead of other areas of expenditure. The social programs are vital for Canada and we should be looking in other areas to save money. We should improve the social programs which provide a safety net for Canadians that is very badly needed.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-PREOCCUPATION OF WOMEN CONCERNING SOCIAL PROGRAMS. (B) NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for her interest in the social programs specifically directed at women.
I would like to take this opportunity to define the principles on which the Government has based its review of social expenditures and the related fiscal provisions announced in the 1986 Budget. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced in his speech, all the measures that will be taken will serve to maintain the universality of social programs, will result in additional resources being directed at the people who need them most, and also will give individuals the opportunity to become self-sufficient; at the same time, the after-tax benefits going to the most affluent who need them least will be reduced.
This review can be described as the next stage in the social program reform initiated by the Government under the double criteria of social responsibility and financial responsibility. Ever since these criteria were announced, the Government of which I am a Member has continued as it had done since the beginning of its mandate to consult the various groups, governments, provinces, and all the other organizations interested in the dossier.
Now, since coming to power, we have initiated a whole series of changes to social measures directed at several groups, including women. For the benefit of my honourable colleague, 1 should like to mention the spouse's allowance which is now granted to all widows and widowers between 60 and 64 years of age, as well as the very important measure which has modified family allowances, again to direct our resources to the most needy families. On the other hand, the principle of universality has always been preserved. Those two measures are especially aimed at women, as we know.
The Government is also proud of the steps it has taken to improve pensions for Canadian women. Women in the labour force will benefit from Government proposals to extend

May 5, 1986
Adjournment Debate
pension plan portability and thereby make them more accessible. Moreover, in order to correct existing discrepancies in the current pension system, of which contributors' spouses are the main victims, and these are mostly women as we know, the Government has taken a number of steps towards pension reform.
For instance, the surviving spouse's pensions will no longer be terminated following a remarriage.
In pension plans, those benefits will have to be guaranteed to surviving spouses of those plan members who were in retirement at time of death.
The total value of pension earned by the contributor who dies before retirement will have to be rolled over into a frozen registered retirement savings plan in the name of the surviving spouse.
Mr. Speaker, several other provisions concerning pension plans have been enacted, and generally those who benefit are

I think, Mr. Speaker, that my time is almost up, but I would quite simply like to suggest while concluding that, in my view, the best kind of income security is still job creation, and this Government, in our job-creation programs, has given tremendous help to Canadian women in a most clear and precise way. I therefore feel that we may be proud of our achievements. This Government will go on, in consultation of course with all interested groups.
